- adaptive: Instructions to make or update an app's UI so that it adapts to different Android devices including phones, tablets, foldables, laptops, desktop, TV, Auto and XR. It includes how to handle different window sizes, pointing devices (such as mouse) and text entry devices (such as keyboard) using the Compose MediaQuery API. It also covers multi-pane layouts using Navigation3 Scenes, adaptive UI components (such as buttons) with varying target sizes, and adaptive layouts (including navigation areas - nav rails and nav bars) using the Compose Grid and FlexBox APIs.
- agp-9-upgrade: Upgrades, or migrates, an Android project to use Android Gradle Plugin (AGP) version 9. Do not use this skill for migrating Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) projects.
- android-cli: Provides instructions for installing and using the `android` CLI. The `android` command-line tool is a critical tool for Android development and helps you create new Android projects, run Android apps on devices, manage and interact with Android virtual devices (including screenshots and UI inspection), manage Android SDK components, look up official Android documentation, and discover and install official Android skills.
- android-intent-security: Best practices for Android Intent security. Use this skill when auditing component configurations in AndroidManifest.xml activities, services, receivers) or source code handling incoming Intents (getIntent, getParcelableExtra) to prevent Intent Redirection and unauthorized access.
- appfunctions: Analyzes Android apps to identify key user workflows for AppFunctions such as creating a note, playing media, or sending an automated or AI agent triggered message, voice commands, or system shortcuts, without needing to open the app UI. Generates Kotlin code to expose these workflows to the Android system, allowing agents to discover and execute them on-device. Also refines KDoc documentation to ensure AI agents correctly understand and use the provided functionality.
- camerax: Provide technical guidance for Android camera development with CameraX. Use when implementing camera features, handling asynchronous recording lifecycles, wiring low-level hardware interop using CameraX, or integrating ML Kit or Media3 effects.
- display-glasses-with-jetpack-compose-glimmer: Provides guidelines for developing projected Android XR apps for display glasses using the Jetpack Compose Glimmer UI toolkit. This skill covers foundational Glimmer design principles, workflows for implementing Jetpack Compose Glimmer, and interaction models for the glasses form factor. Use this skill to build an Android XR Augmented Experience app with Jetpack Compose Glimmer that adheres to the Glimmer design system for optimized glasses styling.
- edge-to-edge: Use this skill to migrate your Jetpack Compose app to add adaptive edge-to-edge support and troubleshoot common issues. Use this skill to fix UI components (like buttons or lists) that are obscured by or overlapping with the navigation bar or status bar, fix IME insets, and fix system bar legibility.
- engage-sdk-integration: Helps developers integrate, debug, and resolve Play Engage SDK implementation issues. Use when adding Engage SDK support, generating publishing code, mapping data classes to entities, or fixing SDK-related errors.
- migrate-xml-views-to-jetpack-compose: Provides a structured workflow for migrating an Android XML View to Jetpack Compose. This skill details the step-by-step process, from planning and dependency setup, to theming and layout migration, validation and XML cleanup. Use this skill when you need to migrate an XML View to Jetpack Compose in an Android project. It solves the problem of converting the UI of a legacy XML View into modern, declarative Compose components while maintaining interoperability.
- navigation-3: Learn how to install and migrate to Jetpack Navigation 3, and how to implement features and patterns such as deep links, multiple backstacks, scenes (dialogs, bottom sheets, list-detail, two-pane, supporting pane), conditional navigation (such as logged-in navigation versus anonymous), returning results from flows, integration with Hilt, ViewModel, Kotlin, and view interoperability.
- perfetto-sql: Translates natural language data intents into syntactically valid Perfetto SQL queries and executes them against a local trace file. Use this skill to extract slice, thread, or memory data from Android Perfetto traces using trace_processor.
- perfetto-trace-analysis: Analyzes Perfetto traces to find the root cause of latency, memory, or jank issues in Android apps. Use when the user provides a Perfetto trace file and asks any question, ongoing investigation, or open-ended request to analyze its contents.
- play-billing-library-version-upgrade: Use this skill when upgrading or migrating an Android project from any legacy Google Play Billing Library (PBL) version to the latest stable version of PBL.
- r8-analyzer: Analyzes Android build files and R8 keep rules to identify redundancies, broad package-wide rules, and rules that subsume library consumer keep rules. Use when developers want to optimize their app's size, remove redundant or overly broad keep rules, or troubleshoot Proguard configurations.
- styles: Use this skill to integrate the Jetpack Compose Styles API into an Android project. This skill guides you through upgrading dependencies, setting up component themes, making custom components styleable, and migrating existing layout properties to use unified styles. Migrate custom design system components, replace hard coded parameters with Style attributes, and use Modifier.styleable for interaction states.
- testing-setup: Analyze and create a testing strategy for native Android apps - install testing libraries, set up test infrastructure, create harnesses for unit tests, UI tests, screenshot tests, and end-to-end tests.
- verified-email: Provides a complete workflow for implementing verified email retrieval on Android Credential Manager API. Use this skill to integrate a secure, OTP-less email verification flow into an Android app. This skill solves the problem of high-friction sign-up processes by leveraging cryptographically verified credentials from trusted providers like Google.
- wear-compose-m3: Expert guidance for working with Wear OS Compose Material3. Use this skill when creating, updating, or migrating Wear OS projects. This includes the androidx.wear.compose.material3, androidx.wear.compose.foundation, and androidx.wear.compose.navigation3 libraries. Also working with core components such as AppScaffold, ScreenScaffold, and TransformingLazyColumn, and core Wear OS concepts such as ambient mode. Migration from lower versions such as Material 2.5 and Horologist.
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- core:architecture-ports: Apply ports & adapters (hexagonal) and clean-architecture rules when designing or reviewing how modules depend on each other — the dependency rule (domain imports no framework), repositories that hide storage, constructor dependency injection, structural interfaces/Protocols over inheritance, single-responsibility services, and DTOs across boundaries instead of ORM rows. Use when adding a service, repository, adapter, port, or handler; when wiring dependencies; when a domain module starts importing a framework/ORM/HTTP/cloud SDK; or when a file mixes business logic with I/O. Do NOT use for pure language-syntax style (types, formatting), test authoring, or security/authz review — those have their own skills.
- core:documentation: Guidance for writing and maintaining project documentation that stays accurate — keep one source of truth and link instead of duplicating, update docs in the same change as the code they describe, co-locate context with the code it explains, maintain a code-to-docs mapping so changes know which doc to touch, and never leave scratch files. Use when adding or editing README/architecture/integration docs, deciding where a piece of documentation belongs, reviewing a PR that changes behavior but not docs, or cleaning up stray notes/TODO files. Do NOT use for API reference auto-generated from code comments, or for code-style/testing rules.
- core:fail-fast: Apply fail-fast error handling — raise immediately on missing or invalid required values instead of returning null/defaults, never swallow exceptions in empty catch blocks, and use typed/custom error classes with actionable context. Use this skill when writing or reviewing error handling, validation, config/parameter reading, try/catch or try/except blocks, or when a defect surfaces far from its cause (works then breaks weirdly later). Trigger keywords — silent fallback, default value, swallowed exception, empty catch, error handling, defensive coding, guard clause. Do NOT use this skill for designing immutable data models (use immutability) or for forward-compatible unused parameters (use forward-compat-slots).
- core:forward-compat-slots: Apply the forward-compatible reserved-injection-slot convention — a constructor or function parameter prefixed with underscore AND typed optional is an intentionally-unused dependency slot kept so future callers can inject it without touching every call site. Use this skill when adding a dependency to a base class or shared signature that not all implementations use yet, when a composing facade must pass the same dependency uniformly to sub-services, when reviewing an unused parameter, or when deciding whether to delete vs keep an unused argument. Trigger keywords — unused parameter, reserved slot, forward compatibility, optional dependency, _logger, _param, injection slot. Do NOT use this skill for general immutability (use immutability) or fail-fast error handling (use fail-fast).
- core:immutability: Minimize mutability — default domain types to immutable, derive new state with copy-on-write instead of mutating in place, never mutate function arguments, and keep a pure functional core with side effects pushed to a thin imperative shell. Use this skill when designing data models, value objects, or state-transition logic; when reviewing code that mutates shared state, reassigns variables, or mutates passed-in arguments; or when separating business logic from I/O. Trigger keywords — mutable state, in-place mutation, copy-on-write, immutable, frozen, readonly, value object, functional core, shared state bug. Do NOT use this skill for error-handling/fallback decisions (use fail-fast) or for reserved unused parameters (use forward-compat-slots).
- core:pr-authoring: Apply evidence-based pull-request authoring practice — keep each change small (~100-300 lines of substantive change) and single-concern, link the issue so your tracker auto-updates, and follow your team's chosen PR workflow and merge style well. This skill presents the trade-offs of mono-PR vs stacked PRs and squash vs merge-commit rather than mandating one (record your team's pick in .claude/rules/team-conventions.md). Use this skill when opening a PR, sizing or splitting a change, naming a branch, writing a PR description, or deciding mono vs stacked. Trigger keywords — open a PR, pull request, branch name, PR description, split this change, change size, mono PR, stacked PR, squash, merge strategy, rebase. Do NOT use this skill for reviewing someone else's PR (use pr-review) or for commit-message wording alone.
- core:pr-review: Apply evidence-based code-review practice when reviewing a pull request or diff — calibrate review depth to the change's risk and blast radius, raise one finding per concern, classify each on a Required/Nit/Question severity ladder, and shape each comment as problem-grounded-in-the-diff then why-it-matters then a concrete fix. Use this skill when reviewing a PR, reading a diff, writing review comments, deciding review depth, triaging which findings block merge, or dispatching per-concern review passes. Trigger keywords — review this PR, code review, review the diff, review comment, severity, required vs nit, blocking finding, reviewer. Do NOT use this skill for authoring/sizing your own PR (use pr-authoring) or for running a specific language's linter/typechecker.
- core:secure-coding: Apply OWASP-based secure-coding rules when writing or reviewing code that handles authorization, secrets, logging, external input, persistence, network calls, or mobile local storage — server-side deny-by-default authz on every object/property/function, no hardcoded secrets (centralized store + rotation), never logging secrets/tokens/PII, validate-and-encode all external input, and mobile OS key stores with no plaintext local storage and TLS. Use when adding an endpoint/handler, an auth or ownership check, a logging statement, a DB or shell query, a config/secret read, an IAM policy, or any mobile data-at-rest code. Do NOT use for architecture/layering design or pure language-style/type rules — those have their own skills. Trigger keywords — SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, IDOR, path traversal, insecure deserialization, hardcoded secret, secret in logs, PII leak, sanitize, encode, deny-by-default authz, input validation, TLS, certificate pinning, Keychain, Keystore, clipboard/screenshot leak, key store.
- core:spec-implement: Orchestrate a tiered generator-verifier loop to implement a tightly-specified change cheaply — a strong-tier orchestrator writes the spec and rules, dispatches the cheap-tier executor agent to generate the code, then dispatches the matching strong-tier review agent to verify it, looping until the verifier is clean. Use when you have a SMALL, well-specified, mechanical implementation task (scaffold a component to a schema, boilerplate to a contract, stubs to a spec) and want to route generation to a cheap model while keeping verification strong. Trigger keywords — implement to spec, scaffold, generate to contract, model routing, cheap generate strong verify, generator-verifier, tiered agents. Do NOT use for ambiguous/design work (do it yourself on the strong model), for trivial one-liners (a single strong pass is cheaper than orchestrating), or for pure review with no generation (use pr-review).
- core:testing-behavior: Guidance for writing and reviewing automated tests that catch real bugs — test observable behavior through public APIs, verify resulting state instead of mock call sequences, write tests that survive refactoring, judge suite strength by mutation rather than coverage %, and treat flaky tests as defects. Use when writing unit/integration tests, deciding what to assert, reviewing a test file or PR's tests, debugging a flaky or brittle test, choosing mocks vs fakes, or interpreting a coverage report. Do NOT use for language-specific test-runner setup (pytest/jest/XCTest config) or for non-test code style.
- kotlin:android-architecture: Native-Android app architecture (Google's recommended layered architecture) — load when reading/writing/reviewing native-Android app/feature module code (androidx.*/android.* imports, Activity/Fragment/Service/ViewModel, an :app or :feature module). Covers the UI/domain/data layers and one-way dependency direction Data <- Domain <- UI; single source of truth (the SSOT owns a data type, exposes it immutably, is its only mutator); unidirectional data flow (state down, events up); keeping app logic out of short-lived OS-owned Activities/Fragments/Services; and confining Context/framework classes behind your own abstractions for testability. Triggers — UI/domain/data layer, ViewModel, repository, single source of truth, SSOT, unidirectional data flow, UDF, Activity, Context. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (use kmp-multiplatform); this is the layering overview, so for depth use android-ui-layer / android-data-layer / android-modularization / jetpack-compose, and for plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-data-layer: Native-Android data layer (repositories + data sources) — load when reading/writing/reviewing a native-Android repository, data source, Room/Retrofit/DataStore class, or DI wiring in an app/feature module. Covers the repository as the data layer's only public API (other layers never touch data sources directly); naming (DataType+Repository; DataType+Source+DataSource e.g. NewsRemoteDataSource); one single source of truth per type (offline-first local DB preferred); suspend for one-shot and Flow for streams; immutable exposed models; main-safety via withContext(ioDispatcher) where Dispatchers.IO IS correct (unlike commonMain); errors as Result/custom exceptions; Hilt constructor injection; fakes over mocks. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (Ktor/SQLDelight/Dispatchers.Default — use kmp-multiplatform/kmp-interop); for the overview use android-architecture, UI state android-ui-layer, modules android-modularization, Compose jetpack-compose, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-modularization: Native-Android Gradle modularization (multi-module app structure) — load when reading/writing/reviewing native-Android module boundaries: Gradle build files (build.gradle(.kts) with implementation/api project dependencies), an :app / :feature / :core / :data module, or navigation between features. Covers low coupling and high cohesion; the common module types (app/feature/data/core); the rule that feature modules never depend on other feature modules (the app module mediates, usually via the navigation graph); keeping each module's public surface minimal with Kotlin internal; preferring Gradle implementation over api to avoid leaking transitive deps; and passing primitive IDs (not whole objects) across boundaries. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain source-set layout (a different axis — use kmp-multiplatform/kmp-structure); for in-app layering use android-architecture, UI state android-ui-layer, repositories android-data-layer, Compose jetpack-compose, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-ui-layer: Native-Android UI-layer state holders (ViewModel + UI state) — load when reading/writing/reviewing a native-Android ViewModel or screen-level state in an app/feature module (androidx.lifecycle.ViewModel / viewModelScope / StateFlow imports; keywords ViewModel, UiState, collectAsStateWithLifecycle, repeatOnLifecycle, main-safe). Covers the ViewModel as screen-level state holder (survives configuration changes, main-safe, holds NO View/Context/lifecycle reference); modeling UI state as one immutable data class (or a sealed UiState when states are genuinely exclusive); exposing it via read-only StateFlow; and consuming it lifecycle-aware via collectAsStateWithLifecycle (Compose) or repeatOnLifecycle (Views) so collection stops in the background. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (use kmp-multiplatform); for the overview use android-architecture, repositories android-data-layer, Compose recomposition/side-effects jetpack-compose, Compose-MP UI kmp-compose-mp-ui, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:jetpack-compose: Native-Android Jetpack Compose UI discipline — load when reading/writing/reviewing @Composable code in a native-Android app/feature module (androidx.compose.* imports). Covers state hoisting (stateless composable, value down / events up); recomposition and stability (@Stable/@Immutable, stable params that let Compose skip, unstable collections, stable lambdas); the side-effect APIs (LaunchedEffect and its key restart, rememberCoroutineScope, DisposableEffect/onDispose, rememberUpdatedState, derivedStateOf, snapshotFlow, produceState); remember vs remember(key) vs rememberSaveable; stable keys for lazy-list items; modifier order and the modifier-parameter convention; slot APIs; previews/testing. Do NOT use for Compose Multiplatform / non-Android targets (Skia canvas, UIKitView, iOS/desktop/web — use kmp-compose-mp-ui) or KMP commonMain shared code (kmp-multiplatform); for the architecture overview use android-architecture, ViewModel/UI-state rules android-ui-layer, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:kmp-compose-mp-ui: Depth guidance for Compose Multiplatform UI across non-Android targets (iOS, desktop, web/Wasm). Covers the central fact that Compose MP renders via a Skiko/Skia canvas, not native UIKit/SwiftUI widgets, and what follows (identical look by default, native-view interop, simulated-native iOS scroll physics since 1.8.0, on-device verification of canvas/interop/accessibility); choosing Compose MP vs native UI per target; stability (iOS Stable since 1.8.0, desktop Stable, Web/Wasm Beta); resources, fonts, density; navigation. Use when building or reviewing shared Compose UI for iOS/desktop/web, deciding Compose MP vs SwiftUI/native, debugging gestures or scroll feel on iOS, handling images/fonts/strings, or wiring shared navigation. Trigger keywords — Compose Multiplatform, Skiko, desktop Compose, Compose for Web, Wasm, UIKitView, compose-resources, navigation. Do NOT use for Android-only Jetpack Compose, non-UI logic (use kmp-structure), or Swift/Kotlin interop (use kmp-interop).
- kotlin:kmp-interop: Depth guidance for Kotlin <-> Swift/Objective-C interop and per-platform networking in KMP. Covers refining the ObjC header Kotlin exports to Swift (@HiddenFromObjC, @ObjCName, @ShouldRefineInSwift), why not to expose Flow directly to Swift (use SKIE) and that suspend->Swift async is officially experimental, exported-surface quirks (top-level funcs become <FileName>Kt classes, generics only on classes, no default args), and Ktor with ktor-client-core in commonMain plus an engine per platform (Darwin/OkHttp/CIO). Use when designing the API a Swift/iOS app consumes from shared Kotlin, debugging an awkward generated Swift signature, deciding how to bridge Flow or suspend to Swift, or wiring the Ktor client. Trigger keywords — Swift interop, Objective-C, @ObjCName, @ShouldRefineInSwift, SKIE, Flow to Swift, suspend async, Ktor, Darwin, OkHttp. Do NOT use for shared logic structure (use kmp-structure), Compose UI (use kmp-compose-mp-ui), or everyday Kotlin language style (use kotlin-style).
- kotlin:kmp-multiplatform: Kotlin Multiplatform framework rules for shared code — load when reading, writing, or reviewing files under a commonMain or commonTest source set (auto-scoped to **/commonMain/**/*.kt and **/commonTest/**/*.kt), or on demand for KMP layout questions. Covers where shared code lives and the one-way platform->common dependency, what to share vs keep native, the commonMain-only coroutine constraint (Dispatchers.Default not IO, because IO is JVM/Native-only and breaks JS/Wasm), the expect/actual escalation ladder, and commonTest using kotlin.test only (no JUnit, which breaks Native). Keywords — KMP, multiplatform, commonMain, commonTest, expect, actual, source set, Dispatchers in common code, JS, Wasm. Do NOT use for native-Android-only code (there Dispatchers.IO is correct — use the android skills), everyday Kotlin language style (kotlin-style), source-set depth (kmp-structure), Compose-MP UI (kmp-compose-mp-ui), or Swift interop (kmp-interop).

Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

1	---
2	name: expect-actual
3	description: Kotlin Multiplatform expect/actual patterns for platform-specific APIs. Learn to declare shared interfaces with platform implementations.
4	---
5	
6	# expect/actual Pattern for KMP
7	
8	The `expect/actual` declaration is Kotlin's mechanism for writing platform-specific implementations while maintaining a shared API surface.
9	
10	## Core Concept
11	
12	```kotlin
13	// shared/commonMain/kotlin/Platform.kt
14	expect class Platform() {
15	    val name: String
16	}
17	
18	// shared/androidMain/kotlin/Platform.android.kt
19	actual class Platform {
20	    actual val name: String = "Android ${Build.VERSION.SDK_INT}"
21	}
22	
23	// shared/iosMain/kotlin/Platform.ios.kt
24	actual class Platform {
25	    actual val name: String = "iOS \(UIDevice.currentDevice.systemVersion)"
26	}
27	```
28	
29	## Common Patterns
30	
31	### 1. Platform Information
32	
33	```kotlin
34	// commonMain
35	expect object Platform {
36	    val name: String
37	    val version: String
38	    val isDebug: Boolean
39	}
40	
41	// androidMain
42	actual object Platform {
43	    actual val name: String = "Android"
44	    actual val version: String = "${Build.VERSION.SDK_INT}"
45	    actual val isDebug: Boolean = BuildConfig.DEBUG
46	}
47	
48	// iosMain
49	actual object Platform {
50	    actual val name: String = "iOS"
51	    actual val version: String = UIDevice.currentDevice.systemVersion
52	    actual val isDebug: Boolean = KotlinLifecycleController.isDebug
53	}
54	```
55	
56	### 2. File System Paths
57	
58	```kotlin
59	// commonMain
60	expect class FileSystem {
61	    fun getDocumentsPath(): String
62	    fun getCachePath(): String
63	    fun getTempPath(): String
64	}
65	
66	// androidMain
67	actual class FileSystem {
68	    actual fun getDocumentsPath(): String {
69	        return context.filesDir.absolutePath
70	    }
71	    actual fun getCachePath(): String {
72	        return context.cacheDir.absolutePath
73	    }
74	    actual fun getTempPath(): String {
75	        return context.cacheDir.absolutePath + "/tmp"
76	    }
77	}
78	
79	// iosMain
80	actual class FileSystem {
81	    actual fun getDocumentsPath(): String {
82	        return NSSearchPathForDirectoriesInDomains(
83	            NSDocumentDirectory,
84	            NSUserDomainMask,
85	            true
86	        ).first() as String
87	    }
88	    actual fun getCachePath(): String {
89	        return NSSearchPathForDirectoriesInDomains(
90	            NSCachesDirectory,
91	            NSUserDomainMask,
92	            true
93	        ).first() as String
94	    }
95	    actual fun getTempPath(): String {
96	        return NSTemporaryDirectory()
97	    }
98	}
99	```
100	
101	### 3. Date/Time Operations
102	
103	```kotlin
104	// commonMain
105	expect class DateTimeFormatter {
106	    fun format(timestamp: Long): String
107	    fun parse(dateString: String): Long
108	    fun now(): Long
109	}
110	
111	// androidMain
112	actual class DateTimeFormatter {
113	    private val format = SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss", Locale.getDefault())
114	
115	    actual fun format(timestamp: Long): String {
116	        return format.format(Date(timestamp))
117	    }
118	
119	    actual fun parse(dateString: String): Long {
120	        return format.parse(dateString)?.time ?: 0L
121	    }
122	
123	    actual fun now(): Long = System.currentTimeMillis()
124	}
125	
126	// iosMain
127	actual class DateTimeFormatter {
128	    private val formatter = NSDateFormatter().apply {
129	        dateFormat = "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
130	    }
131	
132	    actual fun format(timestamp: Long): String {
133	        val date = NSDate(timeIntervalSince1970 = timestamp / 1000.0)
134	        return formatter.stringFromDate(date)
135	    }
136	
137	    actual fun parse(dateString: String): Long {
138	        val date = formatter.dateFromString(dateString) ?: return 0L
139	        return (date.timeIntervalSince1970 * 1000).toLong()
140	    }
141	
142	    actual fun now(): Long = (NSDate().timeIntervalSince1970 * 1000).toLong()
143	}
144	```
145	
146	### 4. Database Paths
147	
148	```kotlin
149	// commonMain
150	expect class DatabasePathProvider {
151	    fun getDatabasePath(name: String): String
152	}
153	
154	// androidMain
155	actual class DatabasePathProvider(private val context: Context) {
156	    actual fun getDatabasePath(name: String): String {
157	        return context.getDatabasePath(name).absolutePath
158	    }
159	}
160	
161	// iosMain
162	actual class DatabasePathProvider {
163	    actual fun getDatabasePath(name: String): String {
164	        val dir = NSSearchPathForDirectoriesInDomains(
165	            NSDocumentDirectory,
166	            NSUserDomainMask,
167	            true
168	        ).first() as String
169	        return "$dir/databases/$name"
170	    }
171	}
172	```
173	
174	### 5. Secure Storage
175	
176	```kotlin
177	// commonMain
178	expect class SecureStorage {
179	    suspend fun save(key: String, value: String)
180	    suspend fun load(key: String): String?
181	    suspend fun delete(key: String)
182	}
183	
184	// androidMain
185	actual class SecureStorage(private val context: Context) {
186	    private val masterKey = MasterKey.Builder(context)
187	        .setKeyScheme(MasterKey.KeyScheme.AES256_GCM)
188	        .build()
189	
190	    private val prefs = EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
191	        context,
192	        "secure",
193	        masterKey,
194	        EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
195	        EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
196	    )
197	
198	    actual suspend fun save(key: String, value: String) {
199	        prefs.edit().putString(key, value).apply()
200	    }
201	
202	    actual suspend fun load(key: String): String? = prefs.getString(key, null)
203	
204	    actual suspend fun delete(key: String) {
205	        prefs.edit().remove(key).apply()
206	    }
207	}
208	
209	// iosMain
210	actual class SecureStorage {
211	    private val keychain = KeychainHelper()
212	
213	    actual suspend fun save(key: String, value: String) {
214	        keychain.set(key, value)
215	    }
216	
217	    actual suspend fun load(key: String): String? {
218	        return keychain.get(key)
219	    }
220	
221	    actual suspend fun delete(key: String) {
222	        keychain.delete(key)
223	    }
224	}
225	```
226	
227	### 6. Network Connectivity
228	
229	```kotlin
230	// commonMain
231	expect class ConnectivityMonitor {
232	    val isOnline: Flow<Boolean>
233	    fun startMonitoring()
234	    fun stopMonitoring()
235	}
236	
237	// androidMain
238	actual class ConnectivityMonitor(private val context: Context) {
239	    private val _isOnline = MutableStateFlow(true)
240	    actual val isOnline: StateFlow<Boolean> = _isOnline.asStateFlow()
241	
242	    private val callback = object : ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback() {
243	        override fun onAvailable(network: Network) {
244	            _isOnline.value = true
245	        }
246	        override fun onLost(network: Network) {
247	            _isOnline.value = false
248	        }
249	    }
250	
251	    actual fun startMonitoring() {
252	        val cm = context.getSystemService(Context.CONNECTIVITY_SERVICE) as ConnectivityManager
253	        cm.registerNetworkCallback(
254	            NetworkRequest.Builder().build(),
255	            callback
256	        )
257	    }
258	
259	    actual fun stopMonitoring() {
260	        val cm = context.getSystemService(Context.CONNECTIVITY_SERVICE) as ConnectivityManager
261	        cm.unregisterNetworkCallback(callback)
262	    }
263	}
264	
265	// iosMain
266	actual class ConnectivityMonitor {
267	    private val _isOnline = MutableStateFlow(true)
268	    actual val isOnline: StateFlow<Boolean> = _isOnline.asStateFlow()
269	
270	    private val monitor = NWPathMonitor()
271	    private val queue = dispatch_queue_create("network", null)
272	
273	    actual fun startMonitoring() {
274	        monitor.pathUpdateHandler = {
275	            _isOnline.value = monitor.currentPath.status == .satisfied
276	        }
277	        monitor.start(queue)
278	    }
279	
280	    actual fun stopMonitoring() {
281	        monitor.cancel()
282	    }
283	}
284	```
285	
286	### 7. Logging
287	
288	```kotlin
289	// commonMain
290	enum class LogLevel { DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR }
291	
292	expect class Logger {
293	    fun log(level: LogLevel, tag: String, message: String, throwable: Throwable?)
294	}
295	
296	// androidMain
297	actual class Logger {
298	    actual fun log(level: LogLevel, tag: String, message: String, throwable: Throwable?) {
299	        when (level) {
300	            LogLevel.DEBUG -> Log.d(tag, message, throwable)
301	            LogLevel.INFO -> Log.i(tag, message, throwable)
302	            LogLevel.WARN -> Log.w(tag, message, throwable)
303	            LogLevel.ERROR -> Log.e(tag, message, throwable)
304	        }
305	    }
306	}
307	
308	// iosMain
309	actual class Logger {
310	    actual fun log(level: LogLevel, tag: String, message: String, throwable: Throwable?) {
311	        val fullMessage = if (throwable != null) "$message: $throwable" else message
312	        println("[$tag] [$level] $fullMessage")
313	        os_log(OSLogDefault, level.toOSLogType(), "%{public}@", fullMessage)
314	}
315	
316	private fun LogLevel.toOSLogType() = when (this) {
317	    LogLevel.DEBUG -> OS_LOG_TYPE_DEBUG
318	    LogLevel.INFO -> OS_LOG_TYPE_INFO
319	    LogLevel.WARN -> OS_LOG_TYPE_DEFAULT
320	    LogLevel.ERROR -> OS_LOG_TYPE_ERROR
321	}
322	```
323	
324	## Best Practices
325	
326	### ✅ DO
327	
328	```kotlin
329	// ✅ Keep expect declarations simple
330	expect class PlatformInfo {
331	    val platform: String
332	}
333	
334	// ✅ Use factory functions for dependencies
335	expect fun createPlatformService(): PlatformService
336	
337	// ✅ Group related functionality
338	expect class FileService {
339	    fun read(path: String): ByteArray
340	    fun write(path: String, data: ByteArray)
341	    fun delete(path: String)
342	}
343	
344	// ✅ Provide default implementations when possible
345	expect class Analytics {
346	    fun track(event: String, properties: Map<String, Any>)
347	    fun flush()
348	}
349	```
350	
351	### ❌ DON'T
352	
353	```kotlin
354	// ❌ Don't add complex logic in expect declarations
355	expect class Platform {
356	    // Complex logic here won't compile
357	    fun calculateSomething(): Int {
358	        // This causes errors
359	    }
360	}
361	
362	// ❌ Don't use expect for pure Kotlin logic
363	// Use commonMain instead
364	expect fun add(a: Int, b: Int): Int  // ❌ This doesn't need expect/actual
365	
366	// ❌ Don't create too many small expect classes
367	// Consolidate related functionality
368	expect class FileReader
369	expect class FileWriter
370	expect class FileDeleter  // ❌ Should be one FileService class
371	```
372	
373	## File Organization
374	
375	```
376	shared/
377	├── commonMain/
378	│   └── kotlin/
379	│       └── com/example/platform/
380	│           ├── Platform.kt          (expect class Platform)
381	│           ├── FileSystem.kt        (expect class FileSystem)
382	│           └── DatabasePath.kt      (expect class DatabasePath)
383	├── androidMain/
384	│   └── kotlin/
385	│       └── com/example/platform/
386	│           ├── Platform.android.kt  (actual class Platform)
387	│           ├── FileSystem.android.kt
388	│           └── DatabasePath.android.kt
389	├── iosMain/
390	│   └── kotlin/
391	│       └── com/example/platform/
392	│           ├── Platform.ios.kt      (actual class Platform)
393	│           ├── FileSystem.ios.kt
394	│           └── DatabasePath.ios.kt
395	└── desktopMain/
396	    └── kotlin/
397	        └── com/example/platform/
398	            ├── Platform.desktop.kt
399	            └── FileSystem.desktop.kt
400	```
401	
402	## Testing with expect/actual
403	
404	```kotlin
405	// commonTest
406	class PlatformTest {
407	    @Test
408	    fun `platform name is not empty`() {
409	        assertTrue(Platform.name.isNotEmpty())
410	    }
411	}
412	
413	// Test runs on all platforms with actual implementations
414	```
415	
416	---
417	
418	**Remember**: Use `expect/actual` only when you truly need platform-specific APIs. Keep as much code as possible in `commonMain`.
419

content.content:
1	---
2	name: kmp-boundaries
3	description: Use when designing Kotlin Multiplatform boundaries — choosing between expect/actual, common interfaces with platform bindings, or separate platform screens. Covers platform services (clipboard, share, haptics, permissions, files, settings, sensors, biometrics), native SDKs, source-set hierarchies (commonMain, skikoMain, appleMain, androidMain), Compose Multiplatform interop, and capability granularity. Use whenever common code needs to reach a platform API and you're picking the boundary shape.
4	---
5	
6	# Kotlin Multiplatform Boundary Design
7	
8	Core rules for any KMP boundary:
9	
10	- **Keep `commonMain` semantic** — describe *what* the product needs, not Android/iOS mechanics: `currentRegion()`, never `currentRegionFromAndroidLocale(context)`.
11	- **Split by capability** — `Clipboard`, `ShareSheet`, `Haptics`, `Biometrics` as separate interfaces, not one `Platform` god object.
12	- **Keep actuals thin** — they translate, they don't decide; a business `if`/`when` inside an actual belongs in common, tested with a fake.
13	- **Prefer a common `interface` + per-platform binding over `expect class`** whenever you need fakes / DI / lifecycle / runtime selection.
14	- **Introduce an intermediate source set** (`skikoMain`, `appleMain`) only when two platforms genuinely share an actual.
15	
16	Two boundaries get the most detail below: the **Activity-owned** platform-UI boundary, and the **AGP-9 KMP-library** constraints.
17	
18	**Related:** `android-skills:kmp-ktor` (network boundary), `compose/references/multiplatform.md` (Compose-MP mechanics), `android-skills:kotlin-coroutines` (scope ownership). For the iOS↔Swift bridge — Kotlin→Swift naming, type widths (`Int` is 32-bit), SKIE `suspend`→`async` / `Flow`→`AsyncSequence`, sealed-class exhaustiveness, SwiftUI embedding — load `references/ios-interop.md` when authoring the iOS-side actual.
19	
20	## Platform-UI bindings are Activity-owned, not Context-owned
21	
22	The single most common Android boundary mistake: passing `applicationContext` / `LocalContext.current` into a binding that actually needs an `Activity`, then papering over the lifecycle gap with `Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK`. That flag is a smell — it hides that this is a foreground-UI operation. Hold an `Activity` instead.
23	
24	```kotlin
25	// commonMain — semantic interface; DOCUMENT what `suspend` means
26	interface ShareSheet {
27	    /** Launches the system share sheet. Returns when the sheet is PRESENTED — not when the user
28	     *  completes or cancels. (Otherwise callers write incorrect retry/confirmation logic.) */
29	    suspend fun shareText(text: String)
30	}
31	
32	// androidMain — thin: build the intent and launch it. Activity-owned.
33	class AndroidShareSheet(private val activity: Activity) : ShareSheet {
34	    override suspend fun shareText(text: String) {
35	        activity.startActivity(Intent.createChooser(
36	            Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).setType("text/plain").putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_TEXT, text), null,
37	        ))
38	    }
39	}
40	```
41	
42	You don't app-wide-inject an `Activity` (it's framework-created and lifecycle-bound) — construct the binding in an **activity scope** in the Android app module (Hilt `@InstallIn(ActivityComponent::class)`, where `Activity` is a default binding; Koin `scoped`). `commonMain` only ever sees the interface; the `Activity` never leaves the app module. If a longer-lived (app-scoped) object needs it, hold it behind a lifecycle-aware provider (set in `onResume`, cleared in `onPause`) so a destroyed Activity can't leak.
43	
44	## AGP-9 KMP-library constraints (structural — they shape what can live in shared code)
45	
46	AGP 9 replaces `com.android.library` with **`com.android.kotlin.multiplatform.library`** for the Android side of a KMP module, and rejects `com.android.application` + `kotlin.multiplatform` outright. The new plugin enforces a single-variant architecture:
47	
48	- **`BuildConfig` is unavailable** — compile-time constants come from [BuildKonfig](https://github.com/yshrsmz/BuildKonfig) or an injected `AppConfiguration` interface. Don't design `commonMain` APIs that assume `BuildConfig.X` exists.
49	- **No build variants** — variant-specific deps/resources/signing live in the app module; a debug/release decision surfaces as a runtime config value injected into common code, not a build-variant split inside the KMP module.
50	- **No NDK / JNI** — extract native (C/C++) into a separate `com.android.library` module, wrapped behind a common interface the KMP module consumes.
51	- **Compose-MP resources need explicit enable** — add `androidResources { enable = true }` inside `kotlin { android { … } }`, or `Res.string.*` / `Res.drawable.*` crash at runtime on Android (the build still succeeds — easy to miss).
52	- **Consumer ProGuard rules need migration** — `consumerProguardFiles("rules.pro")` from the old `android {}` block is silently dropped; use `consumerProguardFiles.add(file("rules.pro"))` in the new DSL.
53	- **The KMP module can't also be `com.android.application`** — the Android entry point (`MainActivity`, Application class, launcher manifest, `applicationId` / `targetSdk` / `versionCode` / `versionName`) moves to a separate `androidApp` module that depends on the shared library. `MainActivity`, app-level Hilt setup, and nav-host wiring all move out of the shared `androidMain`.
54	- **kapt is incompatible** with AGP 9's built-in Kotlin — migrate annotation processors to KSP (2.3.1+), or fall back to `com.android.legacy-kapt` for processors with no KSP equivalent.
55	
56	| Concern | Pre-AGP-9 (monolithic) | AGP 9 KMP library |
57	|---|---|---|
58	| `MainActivity`, Application class, launcher manifest | `androidMain` of shared module | Separate `androidApp` module |
59	| `applicationId`, `versionCode`, `targetSdk` | Shared module's `android {}` | `androidApp` only |
60	| Compile-time constants (env, flags) | `BuildConfig` field | `BuildKonfig` in common, or runtime DI |
61	| NDK / JNI native code | `androidMain` (any module) | Separate `com.android.library`, behind a common interface |
62	
63	For migrating an existing project, see JetBrains' [`kotlin-tooling-agp9-migration`](https://github.com/Kotlin/kotlin-agent-skills/tree/main/skills/kotlin-tooling-agp9-migration) skill for the full mechanics.
64
